title: Śrīdhara Svāmī literal English — Canto 4, chapter 2, checkpoint 1
source_alignment: Śrīdhara's gloss under the source's 4.2.7 heading actually defines the Sanskrit words of 4.2.8 (prāk-niṣaṇṇam, anādṛtaḥ, nāmṛṣyat, vāmam). It is therefore rendered at English 4.2.8, while 4.2.7 has no separately attributable Śrīdhara gloss. His 4.2.15 gloss anticipates the following verse's tamo-mātrātmaka phrase; the latter is rendered under 4.2.16. The source's single grouped gloss on 4.2.27–29 is kept grouped.

entries.text: In the second chapter, the cause of the enmity between Bhava and Dakṣa, mentioned in the first chapter, is described: it arose at the sacrifice of the creators of the world.

Satī means the one named Satī. Nor is he worthy of anyone's hatred; this is stated with ‘Who?’ Who hates him, the teacher of moving and unmoving beings and the deity of the world? How does one hate someone free of enmity? The reason for his freedom from enmity is that he is peaceful; the suffix in śānta has the sense of a state. Peace itself is his form. Why? His delight or affection is in himself alone. Alternatively, ‘Who?’ asks how the progenitor Dakṣa could hate him. Hatred of one possessing these qualities is both unjustified and impossible: this is the meaning.
Tell me what caused the enmity, and from what enmity Satī abandoned her life-breaths. The word ‘from which’ is construed in both places.
To narrate just that, he introduces the history with ‘Formerly.’ ‘Assembled’ means they were gathered together.
‘Entered’ has ‘Dakṣa’ understood as its object. ‘The great assembly’ means the large gathering; ‘from their own stations’ means from their own seats.

‘Seated before’ means Śiva, Mṛḍa, was already sitting before Dakṣa took his own seat. ‘Disrespected by him’ means Śiva did not show him respect by rising and so forth. ‘He did not tolerate’ means he could not bear it. ‘Looking askance’ means looking with his eyes turned obliquely.
‘Let my words be heard.’ He was not speaking out of ignorance or envy.
‘Stiff’ means devoid of appropriate conduct. In the reading ‘destroyed,’ it means ‘fallen from proper conduct.’
He states that very thing with ‘This one’: for he took the hand of my daughter, equal to Sāvitrī, in the presence of the brāhmaṇas and the sacred fire.
She has eyes like those of a deer-calf, a young deer. Although I deserved to be greeted and received by someone rising, he did not show me due honor, not even by words.
Regretting that he gave his daughter to someone unworthy, he speaks with the four and a half verses beginning ‘Whose rites have ceased.’ ‘Desirable speech’ means speech in the form of the Veda.
‘Abodes of the dead’ means cremation grounds. His hair is ‘shorn,’ that is, dishevelled or scattered.

He has bathed in ashes from a funeral pyre. ‘Garlands of the dead’ means garlands belonging to the dead; he has human bones for ornaments. His designation as ‘auspicious’ is a mere name. [The phrase about those whose nature consists solely of darkness is continued in the following verse.]

‘Madmen’ are a particular class of beings, and he is their lord. ‘Of an evil heart’ means ‘of a wicked mind.’ The word bata expresses distress. But the actual meaning is this: rites have ceased in him because he is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman; hence there is none purer than him. One should divide the words as ‘without pride’ and ‘whose boundary has not been broken.’ Thinking, ‘How could my human daughter be fit for that Supreme Lord?’ I was unwilling to give her through shame and the like, but gave her out of desire for that connection. The comparison with a śūdra is only in respect of unworthiness, not inferiority; otherwise it would contradict the speaker's own earlier and later words. Thus, as someone might give a deity to a śūdra out of greed for wealth, so I gave her. Everything beginning with ‘in the abodes of the dead’ is merely a guise: he himself says ‘like a madman’; otherwise he would simply have said ‘a madman.’ ‘Not auspicious’ is to be divided as ‘there is no one more auspicious than him’; ‘intoxicated, fond of intoxicated people’ as ‘not intoxicated, fond of those who are not intoxicated.’ ‘Lord of the hosts of pramathas’ indicates his affection for devotees: he protects even those of dark disposition by removing their faults. Even those who have lost purity derive purity from him. He has the heart that thinks, ‘Even these wicked people deserve my compassion.’ For him, bata expresses joy; the sense is that at Brahmā's word I cast aside shame, fear and the like, and gave [my daughter].
Even though he remained in a way that was not contrary or hostile, Dakṣa reviled him.

At the time of the gods' worship, may he not receive a share along with the gods, but rather receive it before them, since he eats first. Alternatively, let him receive it after they have eaten, since he nourishes everyone. The reason is that he is one beneath whom the hosts of gods stand.
That Dakṣa left that place and went away. ‘O descendant of Kuru’ is the form of address.

‘Foremost among the attendants of Giriśa’ means their chief. Anger itself was the red dye by which he was stained: his eyes were red. ‘Their unspeakable treatment of Giriśa’ means words unfit to address to him, that is, abuse; he also hurled a curse at those [brāhmaṇas].

He curses Dakṣa with three and a half verses. ‘Regarding this mortal’ means regarding Dakṣa's body as the highest thing. ‘One who does no harm in return’ means one who does not retaliate. ‘Seeing separately’ means seeing divisions; ‘from reality’ means from the highest truth.

He further states the condition of ignorance with ‘In houses.’ ‘The apparatus of karma’ means the accessories of ritual action. The Vedic statements, that is, eulogistic statements such as ‘The merit of the performer of the Cāturmāsya rite indeed becomes imperishable,’ have ruined his understanding.

His intellect is accustomed to meditate exclusively upon what is other than the self, such as the body, as though it were the self; by it he has forgotten the self's course, its true nature. Therefore he is like an animal. ‘May he be exceedingly desirous of women’ is the second curse; ‘may his face be the face of a goat’ is the third.

He says that this curse is fitting for him. ‘Having the idea of knowledge in ignorance’ means considering this alone true knowledge; hence he is indeed dull. He curses the twice-born with the two and a half verses beginning ‘May they wander.’ Those who follow that Dakṣa, who despises Śarva, shall wander through birth, death and the like: this is one curse.

The Veda is the heard word. Its ‘flowers’ are its eulogistic statements, because they disturb the mind; that is, it abounds in eulogies. An inducement like the scent of honey, an agitator that stirs the mind, churns their minds. May they become bewildered, that is, attached to ritual acts: this is the second curse.

‘Eaters of everything’ means lacking discrimination between what may and may not be eaten. They have undertaken learning, austerities and vows for a livelihood, to maintain their bodies and so forth. Their enjoyment is in wealth, the body and the senses alone. Let them roam about as beggars: this is a fourfold curse.

Surā is liquor made from jaggery, flour or honey; āsava is alcohol produced from palm and the like. Through the unity of the compound the expression is neuter. ‘Where it is divine’ means where it is worshipped, honored like a deity, or regarded as deserving reverence.
‘Brahman’ means the Veda. What is its nature? It is a boundary, a rule of conduct; he explains this as ‘the support of people,’ sustaining those who practice the duties of varṇa and āśrama.
